eval_factcheck
eval_factcheck

cases.text: TRANSIT, first tested in 1960, was designed and built by NASA.
cases.ai_problem: The cited passage does not mention that NASA designed and built TRANSIT.

cases.text: In 1991, DARPA's small handheld GPS receiver was finished, and it cost less than 1,000 dollars.
cases.ai_problem: The passage does not state that the handheld GPS receiver cost less than 1,000 dollars.
guard: number 1,000 is not in the cited sources

cases.text: Bill Clinton made GPS a dual-use system in 1996 because airlines pushed for it.
cases.ai_problem: The passage does not mention airlines pushing for GPS to become a dual-use system.

cases.text: Qualcomm tested assisted GPS for phones in 2004, and by 2008 it was in every smartphone.
cases.ai_problem: The passage does not state that assisted GPS was in every smartphone by 2008.
guard: number 2008 is not in the cited sources

cases.text: Hydrogen masers are the clocks that keep time inside GPS satellites.
cases.ai_problem: The cited passage does not mention hydrogen masers being used inside GPS satellites.

cases.text: Did you know that more than 6 billion people use GPS every day?
cases.ai_problem: Framing sentence makes a factual claim without cited passages.

cases.text: Today, GPS runs on a constellation of 24 satellites.
cases.ai_problem: Passages state that as of 2026, the GPS constellation has 31 operational satellites rather than 24.

cases.text: Today, GPS is managed by the 50th Space Wing.
cases.ai_problem: Passages state that operation of the GPS constellation was transferred to the U.S. Space Force in 2020.

cases.text: The NIST-F2 caesium clock is the most accurate atomic clock ever built.
cases.ai_problem: Passages state that a trapped aluminium ion optical clock, rather than NIST-F2, set the record for accuracy in 2025.

cases.text: Selective Availability still adds errors of up to 100 metres to civilian GPS signals.
cases.ai_problem: Passages state that Selective Availability was discontinued on May 2, 2000.

cases.text: So far, only 12 GPS satellites broadcast the new L5 signal.
cases.ai_problem: Passage A1.5 states that 21 GPS satellites broadcast L5 signals as of March 2026.

cases.text: The United States' primary time standard is the NIST-F1 caesium clock.
cases.ai_problem: Passage A3.6 states that the United States' primary standard is the NIST-F2 caesium clock, not NIST-F1.

cases.text: In 2009, Air Force Space Command said: "There is no risk at all that GPS will fail."
cases.ai_problem: The quotation is inaccurate; Air Force Space Command stated there was "only a small risk" of not continuing to exceed performance standards.

cases.text: In 2009, the Government Accountability Office said there was "only a small risk" of GPS falling below its standard.
cases.ai_problem: The phrase "only a small risk" was stated by Air Force Space Command, while the Government Accountability Office warned that satellites could fail.

cases.text: A 2015 review praised "the beneficial influence of the Dick effect" on optical clocks.
cases.ai_problem: The 2015 review lamented "the pernicious influence of the Dick effect", rather than praising a beneficial influence.

cases.text: In 1996, Bill Clinton called GPS "a gift to the whole world".
cases.ai_problem: The passage does not record Bill Clinton calling GPS "a gift to the whole world".

cases.text: In 1998, President Al Gore announced two new civilian GPS signals.
cases.ai_problem: Al Gore was Vice President, not President, in 1998.

cases.text: NIST researchers called their record-breaking clock the "quantum leap" clock.
cases.ai_problem: NIST researchers called their clock a "quantum logic" clock, not a "quantum leap" clock.

cases.text: GPS reached initial operational capability in 1995.
cases.ai_problem: sources conflict (A1.32 states December 1993, while X3 states 1995).

cases.text: Only about 20 Atomichron clocks were ever sold.
cases.ai_problem: sources conflict (A3.16 states more than 50 units were sold, while X4 states only about 20 were sold).

cases.text: In total, GPS satellite clocks run fast by about 45 microseconds a day.
cases.ai_problem: sources conflict (A4.64 states 38.6 microseconds per day, while X5 states about 45 microseconds a day).

cases.text: TRANSIT was first successfully tested in 1964.
cases.ai_problem: sources conflict (A1.10 states 1960, while X6 states 1964).

cases.text: International Atomic Time is a weighted average of about 450 clocks.
cases.ai_problem: sources conflict (A3.52 states around 450 clocks, while X7 states about 300 clocks).

cases.text: Bradford Parkinson retired from the Air Force in 1978.
cases.ai_problem: sources conflict (A1.51 states 1978, while X8 states 1980).

cases.text: A timing error of just 1 microsecond puts your position out by about 30 centimetres.
cases.ai_problem: The passage states that an error of 1 nanosecond, not 1 microsecond, corresponds to a positional error of roughly 30 centimetres.
guard: 1 has a different unit in the sources

cases.text: An error of about 10 nanoseconds in the code means a position error of about 3 kilometres.
cases.ai_problem: A 10 nanosecond error corresponds to a positional error of about 3 metres, not 3 kilometres.
guard: 3 has a different unit in the sources

cases.text: Because of their speed, the satellites' clocks fall behind by 7,214 microseconds a day.
cases.ai_problem: The clocks fall behind by 7,214 nanoseconds a day, not microseconds.
guard: 7,214 has a different unit in the sources

cases.text: In 1991, 16-pound military receivers were replaced by a handheld unit of 1.25 kilograms.
cases.ai_problem: The military receivers replaced weighed 16 kilograms (35 pounds), not 16 pounds.
guard: 16 has a different unit in the sources

cases.text: GPS satellites move at 3,874 kilometres per second relative to the centre of the Earth.
cases.ai_problem: GPS satellites move at 3,874 metres per second, not kilometres per second.
guard: 3,874 has a different unit in the sources

cases.text: Strontium optical clocks work at 429 gigahertz.
cases.ai_problem: Strontium optical clocks operate at 429 terahertz, not gigahertz.
guard: 429 has a different unit in the sources

cases.text: TRANSIT, first tested successfully in 1960, used five satellites and gave a position fix about once an hour.
The Gulf War of 1990 to 1991 was the first conflict where the military used GPS widely.
Selective Availability was switched off on 2 May 2000, so civilians everywhere got a clean signal.
In July 2020, the newly created U.S. Space Force took over running the GPS satellites.
A clock that is wrong by just 1 nanosecond puts your position out by roughly 30 centimetres.
Because they move so fast, the satellites' clocks fall behind clocks on Earth by 7,214 nanoseconds every day.
Weaker gravity makes them gain 45,850 nanoseconds a day, so overall they run fast by about 38.6 microseconds daily.
In 1991, a DARPA project shrank military GPS receivers from 16 kilograms to a handheld unit of 1.25 kilograms.
By December 1993, a full set of 24 satellites was in place and GPS reached initial operational capability.
International Atomic Time is a weighted average of around 450 clocks in some 80 institutions.
In 2009, Air Force Space Command said there was "only a small risk" that GPS would stop exceeding its performance standard.
The NIST-F2 caesium clock was developed in 2013, fourteen years after NIST-F1.
Selective Availability once added deliberate errors of up to 100 metres to civilian signals.
Bradford Parkinson spent twenty-one years in the Air Force and retired as a colonel.
Strontium optical clocks work at 429 terahertz, far above the 9.19 gigahertz of caesium clocks.
So how can a clock in space tell you where you are standing?
